title: Always build the dumb baseline first
story:
A score means nothing on its own. It only means something relative to what you would have got without the work, and an astonishing amount of effort is spent producing numbers that nobody ever compared to that floor.

This track has already shown the sharpest case. Where one case in a thousand is positive, the rule that answers negative for every input is correct on 999 of every 1000 — an accuracy of 99.9% — while never identifying a single positive. Anyone reporting that figure without the base rate beside it is reporting the prevalence of the negative class and calling it performance. The baseline is not a formality there; it is the only thing that makes the number readable.

So build the trivial alternative first, before anything else. Predict the majority class. Predict the overall mean. Predict the last observed value, which on anything with time in it is a startlingly hard benchmark to beat. Apply one obvious rule that a domain expert could have written in an afternoon. Each takes minutes, and each produces a number that everything afterwards is measured against.

There are three distinct reasons this earns its place, and only the first is the obvious one.

It makes scores interpretable. Ninety-two percent means nothing until you know the floor is fifty or ninety-one. The interesting quantity was always the gap.

It catches errors that nothing else catches. A pipeline scoring far above its baseline when it should not is a leakage signal, and a pipeline scoring at or below the baseline after weeks of work is a bug report that will otherwise be misread as a hard problem. Both are found immediately and cheaply.

And it repeatedly wins. The evidence in the previous lesson is exactly this experiment run carefully: tree-based models remained state of the art against standard and novel deep learning methods across 45 tabular datasets, even without accounting for their superior speed, and the gap did not close after tuning — a result obtained by actually benchmarking the simpler option instead of assuming it had been superseded. The same logic runs through the discipline of comparison generally; the large cross-validation study concluded that ten-fold stratified cross-validation is best for model selection, which is a statement about how to compare candidates and presupposes that there are candidates to compare against.

The real cost is social rather than technical. The baseline takes an hour and sometimes shows that the simple thing is close enough that the project's premise is in question — which is exactly when you most want to know, and exactly when nobody wants to hear it.

problem.name: The baseline
problem.shape: A model has produced a number, and there is nothing to compare that number against.
tell: a score is quoted with no reference point
months of work have gone in and no trivial alternative was ever fitted
the problem is imbalanced and only accuracy is reported
a result is surprisingly good and nobody has asked why
problem.move: Fit the trivial alternative before anything else and record its score permanently alongside every later one. Use the majority class or the overall mean, the last observed value where the data has time in it, and one obvious hand-written rule. Report every subsequent result as a distance from that floor rather than as a bare number.
problem.invariant: A score is only interpretable relative to what the same data yields with no modelling at all. The quantity of interest is always the gap, never the value.
problem.breaks: A baseline tells you the floor, not the ceiling. Beating it establishes that the model learned something and says nothing about whether the something is enough to be useful, so a comfortable margin over a trivial rule can still be far below what the decision requires.

cost.time: minutes, usually less than the meeting spent discussing whether it is worth doing
cost.beats: reporting bare scores, which are uninterpretable, and discovering after months that a one-line rule was competitive

worked.problem: What does a reported score mean without a baseline beside it?
worked.reasoning:
Very little, and on skewed data it can mean the opposite of what it appears to.

The clean demonstration is the imbalanced one. Where one case in a thousand is positive, the constant rule that always answers negative is correct on 999 of every 1000 — 99.9% — and never identifies a single positive case. That score requires no data, no features and no fitting. So a reported accuracy of 99.9% on such a problem might represent a good model or might represent nothing whatsoever, and the number alone cannot distinguish them. What was always informative is the distance from the floor, and without the floor there is no distance.

That is the interpretability argument, and it is the one people give. There are two more that matter as much in practice.

The second is diagnostic. A baseline turns a scalar into a range with two informative ends. Score far above it and that is a leakage signal worth investigating before celebrating — this track's leakage lesson is the same instinct applied to the same evidence. Score at or below it after weeks of work and you have a bug report, which will otherwise be filed as a hard problem and worked on indefinitely. Both findings arrive within an hour of starting.

The third is that the simple option keeps winning, which is a fact about the world rather than modesty. The tabular benchmark is precisely this experiment conducted carefully: tree-based models remained state of the art against standard and novel deep learning methods across 45 datasets, even without counting their speed advantage, and the gap did not close after tuning. That result exists because somebody benchmarked the simpler option instead of assuming it had been superseded.

A good baseline is problem-shaped rather than generic. Majority class or overall mean for the general case. The last observed value for anything with time in it, which is much harder to beat than people expect. One rule a domain expert would write down unprompted. And where the classes are skewed, the always-negative rule, specifically so that its accuracy is on the record.

The limit I would state is that a baseline gives the floor and not the ceiling. Beating it shows the model learned something; it does not show that the something is sufficient for the decision the model is meant to support, and those are different questions.

problem.practice: Take your current best model and compute three baselines on the same split: the majority class or overall mean, the last observed value if time is involved, and one rule you could write from domain knowledge. Put all four numbers in one table. Then decide whether the gap justifies the complexity you have added.

beats.broke: A score has no meaning on its own, and the number a model reports is routinely accepted as evidence of skill without anything to compare it against.
beats.fix: Build the trivial alternative first — predict the majority class, the overall mean, the last observed value, or a single hand-written rule — and treat its score as the zero point everything else is measured from.
beats.cost: It takes time that feels wasted on a model nobody intends to ship, and it regularly produces the unwelcome result that the trivial alternative is close enough to make the project's premise questionable.

interview.q: What does a reported score mean without a baseline beside it?
interview.trap: Treating the baseline as a courtesy for the write-up. It is diagnostic: scoring far above it is a leakage signal, and scoring at or below it after weeks of work is a bug report that otherwise gets filed as a hard problem.
